content: The formation of a halo surrounding a nevus is thought to occur due to the destruction of melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells of the skin, by CD8+ T lymphocytes, a specific type of white blood cell. The exact trigger for this autoimmune response remains unknown. Halo nevi are estimated to occur in approximately 1% of the general population. This condition affects individuals of all races and sexes equally, although a familial predisposition has been reported. The average age of onset is typically during adolescence. Halo nevi are more commonly observed in individuals with certain conditions, such as vitiligo, malignant melanoma, or Turner syndrome. Halo nevi are characterized by a mole (nevus) surrounded by a depigmented area that resembles a halo. This appearance is the basis for their name. In some cases, the hypopigmented areas may spontaneously regress, with the pigment returning over time. Although halo nevi are benign and pose no direct harm, it is crucial to monitor the lesions regularly. Any changes in the appearance of existing or new halo nevi should be documented. If changes are accompanied by symptoms such as pain, itching, or signs of infection, immediate medical consultation is necessary to rule out the possibility of melanoma. Since halo nevi are of cosmetic concern only, no treatment is required. Patients with halo nevi are typically asymptomatic.
